thread.title: Judge Oldham Roasts Biden's Stove Rule Harder Than Any Stove Ever Could
thread.title_full: Judge Oldham Roasts Biden's Stove Rule Harder Than Any Stove Ever Could

author: Mark
title: Judge Oldham Roasts Biden's Stove Rule Harder Than Any Stove Ever Could
text:
A three-judge panel on the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals just handed down a unanimous 3-0 decision voiding the Biden administration's energy efficiency standards for consumer stoves and ovens. The opinion, authored by Judge Andrew Oldham — a Trump appointee sitting in New Orleans — didn't just strike the rule down. It dismantled it with the kind of dry judicial humor that makes you want to frame the opinion and hang it in your kitchen.
The rule in question was a set of efficiency standards the Department of Energy pushed through in August 2024 using something called a Direct Final Rule — a procedural shortcut that lets agencies skip the standard notice-and-comment process. The idea is that a DFR is reserved for non-controversial, routine regulatory housekeeping. The DOE apparently looked at the most politically explosive appliance regulation in recent memory and thought, yeah, this qualifies.
Seven states — Louisiana, Mississippi, Montana, Nebraska, Tennessee, Texas, and Utah — disagreed and sued. Judge Oldham agreed with every word of their argument.
His opinion is worth reading in full, but here are the highlights. On the DOE's claim that the rule was non-controversial enough for the DFR shortcut, Oldham wrote that "it cannot be contended with a straight face" that seven states opposing the rule didn't constitute significant controversy. He noted that the DOE had already tried to push similar stove efficiency standards in 2023 and generated massive public backlash — then turned around and used the DFR process to avoid hearing from the public a second time.
Oldham described the regulations as making stoves "more expensive and less useful." Six words. That's the whole Biden energy agenda in a nutshell.
But the real gem came when the DOE tried to argue that withdrawing a previous version of the rule and reissuing it as a DFR somehow revived its legal authority. Oldham wasn't having it: "Going from dead to alive is the great promise of Holy Scripture, but the Department cites no authority for its relevance to administrative law."
That's a sitting federal judge comparing the DOE's legal theory to the Resurrection — and finding the DOE's version less credible.
Energy Secretary Chris Wright, who inherited the mess from the previous administration, had already signaled the Trump administration's position back in July 2026, saying the Biden-era standards would "raise costs and disrupt consumer choice." The court's ruling now makes it official: the standards are dead.
The open-borders-to-your-kitchen crowd will point out that efficiency standards are routine and that the DOE has broad authority over appliances. Which is true — when the agency follows its own rules. The entire basis of this ruling isn't that the government can never regulate stoves. It's that you can't use a procedural shortcut designed for uncontested rules to ram through one of the most publicly contested regulatory actions in recent DOE history. That's not efficiency. That's evasion.
This fits a pattern we've seen across the Biden regulatory apparatus: propose something unpopular, get pushback, then find a procedural back door to do it anyway. The courts keep catching it. The 5th Circuit alone has now blocked multiple attempts to bypass public comment periods.
The decision is unanimous, the reasoning is airtight, and the opinion reads like it was written by someone who genuinely enjoyed the work.
The DOE spent two years trying to make your stove worse and hoping you wouldn't notice. Three judges in New Orleans noticed.
summary: Circuit Court of Appeals just handed down a unanimous 3-0 decision voiding the Biden administration's energy efficiency standards for consumer stoves and ovens. But the real gem came when the DOE tried to argue that withdrawing a previous version of the rule and reissuing it as a DFR somehow revived its legal authority. Oldham wasn't having it: "Going from dead to alive is the great promise of Holy Scripture, but the Department cites no authority for its relevance to administrative law."
